newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Pressure mounts on PNG to end mercenary plan.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on PNG to end mercenary plan.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday stepped up its diplomatic campaign against Papua New Guinea's plan to use mercenaries on Bougainville, summoning Port Moresby's top diplomat in for a protest and demanding a detailed explanation.

Papua New Guinea church and political leaders also voiced their opposition to plans to send mercenaries into secessionist Bougainville as military advisors, saying such a move would "legitimise the culture of violence" on the island.

Meanwhile Amnesty International, which reported that government troops were responsible for more than 40 deaths and "disappearances" last year on Bougainville, warned the use of mercenaries would led to a dramatic rise in human rights abuses.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told parliament on Wednesday that he had urged other nations, including Britain, New Zealand and the United States, to voice their concerns to Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.

"This morning, I called into my office the Papua New Guinea high commissioner to make clear our concerns again and to seek urgently clarification from the Papua New Guinea government," Downer said. The high commissioner is the equivalent among British Commonwealth countries of an ambassador.
Canberra has warned Port Moresby that using mercenaries to quell the nine-year secessionist rebellion would harm its international reputation.
On Tuesday, Papua New Guinea admitted it had hired mercenaries to accompany local troops on a mission against secessionist rebels on Bougainville -- but only as advisors.
Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan said the operation would last a year and cost around A$36 million (US$27 million).
Amnesty International warned that the use of mercenaries for either training or fighting would result in an increase in human rights abuses, citing similar conflicts in Angola and Namibia.
"Amnesty International is extremely concerned about the prospect of mercenaries being used in any conflict, particularly in Bougainville," Amnesty spokesman Malcolm Reid told Reuters.
"We believe quite strongly that it can only inflame the situation," Reid said.

The London-based human rights organisation reported that the Papua New Guinea Defence Force and the paramilitary Resistance Forces were responsible for 44 "unlawful or indiscriminate killings or 'disappearances'" last year.
John Momis, MP on Bougainville, said mercenaries would "legitamise the culture of violence" on Bougainville and the island's Catholic archbishop asked Chan not to use mercenaries.
"I beg the government not to be misled into thinking this would be a legitimate or sensible response to the tragedy of Bougainville," archbishop Karl Hesse said in a statement.

Moses Havini, the Sydney-based spokesman for the rebel's Bougainville Interim Government, said the use of mercenaries had ended any chance of peace and rejected assurances the "soldiers of fortune" would only be used as military advisors.
"This is exactly what the Americans did in the Vietnam War," Havini told Reuters.
"It's utterly annihilated the peace process. How can we talk peace with him (Chan) when he has these mercenaries."
